# Sirach Chapter 5 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Sirach 5 (15 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 12

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.1: "set your heart on your wealth" vs. "rely on your wealth"

**EMET:** "Do not set your heart on your wealth"
**LOGOS:** "Do not rely on your wealth"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't build your life on what you own"
**Issue:** Greek epi tois chrēmasin sou mē epistērizou = "do not lean/rely on your wealth." LOGOS is more literal to "lean upon." EMET's "set your heart" conveys emotional attachment. Consensus: "Do not set your heart on your wealth."

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.2: "inclination and your strength" vs. "impulses and your own strength"

**EMET:** "Do not follow your inclination and your strength"
**LOGOS:** "Do not be led by your impulses and your own strength"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't let your impulses and your own desires call the shots"
**Issue:** Greek en tē hormai kardias sou = "in the impulse of your heart." "Inclination" (EMET) is acceptable but "impulse" (LOGOS) is more forceful. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.3: "exact retribution" vs. "bring you to account"

**EMET:** "the Lord will indeed exact retribution"
**LOGOS:** "the Lord will surely bring you to account"
**PNEUMA:** "the Lord will hold you accountable"
**Issue:** Greek ekdikēsei se = "will avenge/take vengeance on you." EMET's "exact retribution" is more juridical. LOGOS "bring to account" is slightly softer. Consensus: "the Lord will surely bring you to account."

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.4: Addition of "but do not presume on his patience"

**EMET:** does not add this phrase
**LOGOS:** adds "but do not think he is indifferent"
**PNEUMA:** adds "patient is not the same as blind"
**Issue:** All three agents note that v.4 in the Greek is simply "for the Lord is slow to anger" — but the context demands the implicit warning be stated. LOGOS and PNEUMA both add clarifying phrases not in the Greek text. Consensus: add a brief clarification but flag it as interpretive: "but do not presume on his patience."

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.5: "confident in atonement" vs. "presumptuous about forgiveness"

**EMET:** "Do not be so confident in atonement"
**LOGOS:** "Do not be so presumptuous about forgiveness"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't presume on forgiveness"
**Issue:** Greek exhilasmos = "atonement/propitiation." EMET is most literal. LOGOS/PNEUMA read functionally. Consensus: "Do not be so confident in forgiveness that you pile sin upon sin."

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.6: "both mercy and wrath are with him" vs. "with him are both mercy and wrath"

**EMET:** "both mercy and wrath are with him"
**LOGOS:** "with him are both mercy and wrath"
**PNEUMA:** "Yes, he is merciful — but he is also capable of wrath"
**Issue:** PNEUMA paraphrases significantly, diluting the parallelism. EMET and LOGOS are nearly identical in content. Consensus: "for with him are both mercy and wrath."

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.7: "put it off from day to day" vs. "postpone it day after day"

**EMET:** "do not put it off from day to day"
**LOGOS:** "do not postpone it day after day"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't say, 'I'll do it tomorrow, and the day after'"
**Issue:** Greek mē anterizou eis hemeran ex hēmeras = "do not delay from day to day." PNEUMA expands the saying. Consensus: "do not postpone it from day to day."

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.9: "winnow in every wind" vs. "scatter yourself with every wind"

**EMET:** "Do not winnow in every wind"
**LOGOS:** "Do not scatter yourself with every wind"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't shift with every wind"
**Issue:** Greek en panti anemō mē pneō = variant; main Greek has "do not sift/fan with every wind." EMET preserves the agricultural image (winnowing = separating grain with wind). This is more literal and more vivid. Consensus: "Do not winnow with every wind."

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.9: "double-tongued sinner" vs. "duplicitous"

**EMET:** "the way of the double-tongued sinner"
**LOGOS:** "the way of the duplicitous"
**PNEUMA:** "people who say one thing and mean another"
**Issue:** Greek diglōssos = "two-tongued." Ben Sira uses this term frequently as a technical category. "Double-tongued" preserved in consensus. "Sinner" is not explicit in the Greek at this point. Consensus: "the way of the double-tongued."

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.11: "be swift to hear" vs. "be quick to hear"

**EMET:** "Be swift to hear"
**LOGOS:** "Be quick to listen"
**PNEUMA:** "Listen fast"
**Issue:** Greek taxys eis tēn akoēn = "swift to hearing." All capture the meaning. "Quick to hear" is the more recognized phrasing (cf. Jas 1:19). Consensus: "Be quick to hear."

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.12: "a person's tongue can be his downfall" vs. "ruin"

**EMET:** "a person's tongue can be his downfall"
**LOGOS:** "a person's tongue can be his ruin"
**PNEUMA:** "The same tongue that wins you honor can ruin you"
**Issue:** Greek hē glōssa autou ptōma autō = "his tongue is his fall." Minor. Consensus: "a person's tongue can be his ruin."

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.13: "gossip" vs. "one who spreads rumors"

**EMET:** "Do not be called a gossip"
**LOGOS:** "Do not earn the name of gossip"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't get a reputation as a gossip"
**Issue:** Greek psithuristēs = "whisperer/gossip." All three use "gossip." The nuance is "whisperer" — one who gossips under the radar. "Gossip" is adequate. Consensus: LOGOS — "Do not earn the name of gossip."

---
